claim: Human cerebral organoids develop progenitor-rich zones akin to ventricular zones from which neuronal progenitors differentiate and migrate radially.
source: Human cerebral organoids are unique in their development of progenitor-rich zones akin to ventricular zones from which neuronal progenitors differentiate and migrate radially.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Lancaster et al., 2013; Qian et al., 2016; Paşca et al., 2015; Mariani et al., 2012; Kadoshima et al., 2013) and is consistent with established knowledge about organoid development.

claim: Analyses of cerebral organoids have been limited to sectioned tissue or superficial layers due to high scattering properties.
source: Analyses of cerebral organoids thus far have been performed in sectioned tissue or in superficial layers due to their high scattering properties.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Lancaster et al., 2013; Paşca et al., 2015; Bershteyn et al., 2017; Klaus et al., 2019; Birey et al., 2017; Birey et al., 2022; Xiang et al., 2017; Mansour et al., 2018) and represents a limitation in the field.

claim: Label-free three-photon imaging can assess intact cerebral organoids to approximately 2 mm depth.
source: Here, we demonstrate label-free three-photon imaging of whole, uncleared intact organoids (~2 mm depth) to assess early events of early human brain development.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing imaging depth capabilities.

claim: Rett Syndrome mutant organoids show defects in ventricular zone volumetric structure compared to isogenic control organoids.
source: Optimizing a custom-made three-photon microscope to image intact cerebral organoids generated from Rett Syndrome patients, we show defects in the ventricular zone volumetric structure of mutant organoids compared to isogenic control organoids.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4 showing quantitative differences in VZ structure.

claim: Mutant radially migrating neurons have shorter migration distances compared to control neurons.
source: Long-term imaging live organoids reveals that shorter migration distances and slower migration speeds of mutant radially migrating neurons are associated with more tortuous trajectories.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from live cell tracking presented in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Mutant radially migrating neurons have slower migration speeds compared to control neurons.
source: Long-term imaging live organoids reveals that shorter migration distances and slower migration speeds of mutant radially migrating neurons are associated with more tortuous trajectories.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from live cell tracking presented in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Mutant radially migrating neurons have more tortuous trajectories compared to control neurons.
source: Long-term imaging live organoids reveals that shorter migration distances and slower migration speeds of mutant radially migrating neurons are associated with more tortuous trajectories.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from live cell tracking presented in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Human cerebral organoids recapitulate gene expression programs of the fetal cortex.
source: Human cerebral organoids also recapitulate gene expression programs of the fetal cortex (Qian et al., 2016; Velasco et al., 2019; Quadrato et al., 2017; Pollen et al., 2019; Luo et al., 2016; Camp et al., 2015) as well as the fetal brain epigenome (Luo et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work demonstrating gene expression similarities.

claim: Human cerebral organoids recapitulate the fetal brain epigenome.
source: Human cerebral organoids also recapitulate gene expression programs of the fetal cortex (Qian et al., 2016; Velasco et al., 2019; Quadrato et al., 2017; Pollen et al., 2019; Luo et al., 2016; Camp et al., 2015) as well as the fetal brain epigenome (Luo et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Luo et al., 2016).

claim: Cerebral organoids have been used to model microcephaly.
source: Thus, they have been used to model neurogenesis-relevant human pathologies such as microcephaly (Lancaster et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2019), licencephaly (Bershteyn et al., 2017), heterotopia (Klaus et al., 2019), Zika virus infection (Qian et al., 2016; Garcez et al., 2016; Dang et al., 2016), and idiopathic autism (Mariani et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work using organoids to model microcephaly.

claim: Cerebral organoids have been used to model lissencephaly.
source: Thus, they have been used to model neurogenesis-relevant human pathologies such as microcephaly (Lancaster et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2019), licencephaly (Bershteyn et al., 2017), heterotopia (Klaus et al., 2019), Zika virus infection (Qian et al., 2016; Garcez et al., 2016; Dang et al., 2016), and idiopathic autism (Mariani et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Bershteyn et al., 2017).

claim: Cerebral organoids have been used to model heterotopia.
source: Thus, they have been used to model neurogenesis-relevant human pathologies such as microcephaly (Lancaster et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2019), licencephaly (Bershteyn et al., 2017), heterotopia (Klaus et al., 2019), Zika virus infection (Qian et al., 2016; Garcez et al., 2016; Dang et al., 2016), and idiopathic autism (Mariani et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Klaus et al., 2019).

claim: Cerebral organoids have been used to model Zika virus infection.
source: Thus, they have been used to model neurogenesis-relevant human pathologies such as microcephaly (Lancaster et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2019), licencephaly (Bershteyn et al., 2017), heterotopia (Klaus et al., 2019), Zika virus infection (Qian et al., 2016; Garcez et al., 2016; Dang et al., 2016), and idiopathic autism (Mariani et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Qian et al., 2016; Garcez et al., 2016; Dang et al., 2016).

claim: Cerebral organoids have been used to model idiopathic autism.
source: Thus, they have been used to model neurogenesis-relevant human pathologies such as microcephaly (Lancaster et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2019), licencephaly (Bershteyn et al., 2017), heterotopia (Klaus et al., 2019), Zika virus infection (Qian et al., 2016; Garcez et al., 2016; Dang et al., 2016), and idiopathic autism (Mariani et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Mariani et al., 2015).

claim: Rett Syndrome is an X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder caused by mutations in the gene encoding MeCP2.
source: Rett Syndrome (RTT) is an X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder caused by mutations in the gene encoding Methyl CpG binding protein 2 (MeCP2).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Rett Syndrome.

claim: MeCP2 is a pleiotropic regulator of gene expression that impacts multiple components of brain development and function.
source: MeCP2 is a pleiotropic regulator of gene expression and impacts multiple components of brain development and function (Ip et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Ip et al., 2018).

claim: Postmortem RTT human brains show reduced cortical thickness.
source: Structural deficits described in postmortem RTT human brains include reduced cortical thickness, cell size and dendritic arborization (Armstrong et al., 1995; Bauman et al., 1995) and reduced cerebral volume in MR imaging of RTT patients (Carter et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Armstrong et al., 1995; Bauman et al., 1995).

claim: Postmortem RTT human brains show reduced cell size.
source: Structural deficits described in postmortem RTT human brains include reduced cortical thickness, cell size and dendritic arborization (Armstrong et al., 1995; Bauman et al., 1995) and reduced cerebral volume in MR imaging of RTT patients (Carter et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Armstrong et al., 1995; Bauman et al., 1995).

claim: Postmortem RTT human brains show reduced dendritic arborization.
source: Structural deficits described in postmortem RTT human brains include reduced cortical thickness, cell size and dendritic arborization (Armstrong et al., 1995; Bauman et al., 1995) and reduced cerebral volume in MR imaging of RTT patients (Carter et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Armstrong et al., 1995; Bauman et al., 1995).

claim: RTT patients show reduced cerebral volume in MR imaging.
source: Structural deficits described in postmortem RTT human brains include reduced cortical thickness, cell size and dendritic arborization (Armstrong et al., 1995; Bauman et al., 1995) and reduced cerebral volume in MR imaging of RTT patients (Carter et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Carter et al., 2008).

claim: RTT mouse models show reductions in dendritic arborization.
source: These deficits are paralleled by reductions in dendritic arborization, soma size and spine density described in RTT mouse models (Fukuda et al., 2005; Kishi and Macklis, 2004; Shahbazian et al., 2002; Smrt et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Fukuda et al., 2005; Kishi and Macklis, 2004; Shahbazian et al., 2002; Smrt et al., 2007).

claim: RTT mouse models show reductions in soma size.
source: These deficits are paralleled by reductions in dendritic arborization, soma size and spine density described in RTT mouse models (Fukuda et al., 2005; Kishi and Macklis, 2004; Shahbazian et al., 2002; Smrt et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Fukuda et al., 2005; Kishi and Macklis, 2004; Shahbazian et al., 2002; Smrt et al., 2007).

claim: RTT mouse models show reductions in spine density.
source: These deficits are paralleled by reductions in dendritic arborization, soma size and spine density described in RTT mouse models (Fukuda et al., 2005; Kishi and Macklis, 2004; Shahbazian et al., 2002; Smrt et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Fukuda et al., 2005; Kishi and Macklis, 2004; Shahbazian et al., 2002; Smrt et al., 2007).

claim: 2D human stem cell models of RTT show aberrant transcription.
source: 2D human stem cell models of RTT, generated by reprogramming of patient cells or genome editing, have revealed deficits in human RTT neurons including aberrant transcription (Lyst and Bird, 2015; Li et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2013; Gomes et al., 2020; Trujillo et al., 2021), impaired neuronal maturation and electrophysiological function (Li et al., 2013; Tang et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2011; Farra et al., 2012), and up- or down-regulation of key signaling pathways and activity-related genes (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Lyst and Bird, 2015; Li et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2013; Gomes et al., 2020; Trujillo et al., 2021).

claim: 2D human stem cell models of RTT show impaired neuronal maturation and electrophysiological function.
source: 2D human stem cell models of RTT, generated by reprogramming of patient cells or genome editing, have revealed deficits in human RTT neurons including aberrant transcription (Lyst and Bird, 2015; Li et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2013; Gomes et al., 2020; Trujillo et al., 2021), impaired neuronal maturation and electrophysiological function (Li et al., 2013; Tang et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2011; Farra et al., 2012), and up- or down-regulation of key signaling pathways and activity-related genes (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Li et al., 2013; Tang et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2011; Farra et al., 2012).

claim: 2D human stem cell models of RTT show up- or down-regulation of key signaling pathways and activity-related genes.
source: 2D human stem cell models of RTT, generated by reprogramming of patient cells or genome editing, have revealed deficits in human RTT neurons including aberrant transcription (Lyst and Bird, 2015; Li et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2013; Gomes et al., 2020; Trujillo et al., 2021), impaired neuronal maturation and electrophysiological function (Li et al., 2013; Tang et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2011; Farra et al., 2012), and up- or down-regulation of key signaling pathways and activity-related genes (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Li et al., 2013).

claim: 3D cerebral organoids from RTT patients show impaired proliferation of the progenitor pool.
source: Using fixed tissue slices from 3D cerebral organoids, we have recently demonstrated impaired proliferation of the progenitor pool and delayed maturation and presumed migration of neurons (Mellios et al., 2011), consistent with human postmortem deficits.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors (Mellios et al., 2011).

claim: 3D cerebral organoids from RTT patients show delayed maturation and presumed migration of neurons.
source: Using fixed tissue slices from 3D cerebral organoids, we have recently demonstrated impaired proliferation of the progenitor pool and delayed maturation and presumed migration of neurons (Mellios et al., 2011), consistent with human postmortem deficits.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors (Mellios et al., 2011).

claim: The majority of analyses of cerebral organoids have been performed in sectioned tissue.
source: The majority of analyses of cerebral organoids have been performed in sectioned tissue (Bershteyn et al., 2017; Klaus et al., 2019; Li et al., 2011; Lancaster and Knoblich, 2014; Andersen et al., 2020; Bagley et al., 2017; Karzbrun et al., 2018; Lancaster et al., 2017; Miura et al., 2020), although recent progress has been made in studying migration using labeled neurons in organoid models (Klaus et al., 2019; Bagley et al., 2017; Birey et al., 2017; Birey et al., 2022; Xiang et al., 2017; Bajaj et al., 2021), including assembloid preparations (Birey et al., 2017; Birey et al., 2022; Xiang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Labeled live cell imaging generally requires phototoxic dyes and limited incubation conditions.
source: However, labeled live cell imaging generally requires phototoxic dyes and limited incubation conditions, and results as well in labeling mostly peripheral neurons and cells which are not ideal for long-term imaging and for finding ventricular like zones in 3D intact organoids.
evidence: This claim is based on general knowledge about limitations of fluorescent labeling methods.

claim: Cerebral organoids appear opaque due to the optical density of neuronal tissues and the large number of apoptotic cells in the center.
source: Optically, cerebral organoids appear opaque due to the optical density of neuronal tissues and the large number of apoptotic cells in the center of 3D intact conditions (Lancaster and Knoblich, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Lancaster and Knoblich, 2014).

claim: THG signal is generated at structural interfaces such as local transitions of the refractive index or inside materials with higher third order nonlinear susceptibility.
source: THG signal is either generated at structural interfaces such as local transitions of the refractive index or inside the materials whose third order nonlinear susceptibility χ3 is higher.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the physical basis of THG signal generation.

claim: THG excitation of biological tissues occurs predominantly at interfaces between aqueous interstitial fluids and lipid-rich structures.
source: Thus, THG excitation of biological tissues occurs predominantly at interfaces that are formed between aqueous interstitial fluids and lipid-rich structures, such as cellular membrane (Rehberg et al., 2011) and lipid bodies (Débarre et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Rehberg et al., 2011; Débarre et al., 2006).

claim: THG microscopy provides label-free structural brain imaging without problems of phototoxicity and photobleaching.
source: In contrast, THG microscopy provides label-free structural brain imaging (Yildirim et al., 2020) without problems of phototoxicity and photobleaching - which are its strengths for long-term live cell imaging of cerebral organoids.
evidence: This claim is based on the physical properties of THG imaging and is supported by citation (Yildirim et al., 2020).

claim: THG microscopy has been applied to non-invasive monitoring of human adipose tissue.
source: THG microscopy has been applied recently to the non-invasive monitoring of human adipose tissue (Chang et al., 2013), cell nuclei and cytoplasm in liver tissue (Lin et al., 2014) and subcortical structures within an intact mouse brain (Yildirim et al., 2019; Ouzounov et al., 2017; Yildirim et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Chang et al., 2013).

claim: THG microscopy has been applied to imaging cell nuclei and cytoplasm in liver tissue.
source: THG microscopy has been applied recently to the non-invasive monitoring of human adipose tissue (Chang et al., 2013), cell nuclei and cytoplasm in liver tissue (Lin et al., 2014) and subcortical structures within an intact mouse brain (Yildirim et al., 2019; Ouzounov et al., 2017; Yildirim et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Lin et al., 2014).

claim: THG microscopy has been applied to imaging subcortical structures within an intact mouse brain.
source: THG microscopy has been applied recently to the non-invasive monitoring of human adipose tissue (Chang et al., 2013), cell nuclei and cytoplasm in liver tissue (Lin et al., 2014) and subcortical structures within an intact mouse brain (Yildirim et al., 2019; Ouzounov et al., 2017; Yildirim et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Yildirim et al., 2019; Ouzounov et al., 2017; Yildirim et al., 2020).

claim: The ventricular zone in RTT mutant organoids has larger volume compared to isogenic control organoids.
source: Comparing organoids from RTT patients and isogenic controls, we show that the ventricular zone in mutant organoids has larger volume, larger surface area, and lower ventricular thickness compared to isogenic control organoids.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: The ventricular zone in RTT mutant organoids has larger surface area compared to isogenic control organoids.
source: Comparing organoids from RTT patients and isogenic controls, we show that the ventricular zone in mutant organoids has larger volume, larger surface area, and lower ventricular thickness compared to isogenic control organoids.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: The ventricular zone in RTT mutant organoids has lower ventricular thickness compared to isogenic control organoids.
source: Comparing organoids from RTT patients and isogenic controls, we show that the ventricular zone in mutant organoids has larger volume, larger surface area, and lower ventricular thickness compared to isogenic control organoids.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: The custom three-photon microscope uses moderate repetition rate (<1 MHz) to maximize energy per pulse and reduce average laser power requirement.
source: First, we utilized moderate repetition rate (<1 MHz) to maximize the energy per pulse and reduce the average laser power requirement for THG imaging.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design and optimization of the microscope system.

claim: The pulse width on the sample was reduced to 27 fs in the deepest part of the organoids.
source: The pulse width on the sample was reduced to 27 fs in the deepest part of the organoids (see Materials and methods) enabling us to further reduce the average power requirement by two- to threefold compared to other three-photon studies in the literature (Yildirim et al., 2019; Ouzounov et al., 2017; Weisenburger et al., 2019; Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: The optimized optical design reduced the average power requirement by two- to threefold compared to other three-photon studies.
source: The pulse width on the sample was reduced to 27 fs in the deepest part of the organoids (see Materials and methods) enabling us to further reduce the average power requirement by two- to threefold compared to other three-photon studies in the literature (Yildirim et al., 2019; Ouzounov et al., 2017; Weisenburger et al., 2019; Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing the current system to prior work, shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: The optical design increased the collected signal by twofold compared to off-the-shelf optics.
source: This optical design procedure enabled us to reduce the spherical aberration in the system and increase the collected signal by twofold compared to off-the shelf optics (Ouzounov et al., 2017; Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: After 35 days of culture, cerebral organoids demonstrated formation of well-organized structures composed of a VZ-like layer around a ventricle-like cavity and a surrounding CP-like structure.
source: In accordance with previous studies (Lancaster et al., 2013; Qian et al., 2016; Velasco et al., 2019), after 35 days of culture, the cerebral organoids demonstrated formation of well-organized structures composed of a ventricular zone (VZ)-like layer (KI67-positive proliferative cells) around a ventricle-like cavity and a surrounding cortical plate (CP)-like structure (Tuj1 or DCX-positive neurons) (Figure 2A–B, see details of the generation of organoids in Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-B and citations to prior work (Lancaster et al., 2013; Qian et al., 2016; Velasco et al., 2019).

claim: CP and VZ substructures demonstrated distinct cell density and morphology.
source: Notably, CP and VZ substructures demonstrated distinct cell density and morphology as shown by nuclear (7AAD) stain and plasma membrane specific dye (WGA) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The VZ region is densely populated by neural progenitor cells and few immature neurons.
source: The VZ region, densely populated by neural progenitor cells and few immature neurons, could be markedly distinguished from the CP substructure with a less dense population of neurons.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations and established knowledge about VZ composition.

claim: THG imaging provided a clean delineation between VZ and CP with lower signal intensity in VZ than CP.
source: Strikingly, THG imaging provided a clean delineation between VZ and CP as THG signal intensity was lower in the former area than the latter (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: The intrinsic THG signal mostly arose distinctly from cell membranes.
source: The intrinsic THG signal mostly arose distinctly from cell membranes.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations and knowledge about THG signal generation.

claim: THG signal revealed the typical radially elongated and bipolar radial glia cell morphology.
source: Consequently, the THG signal nicely revealed the typical radially elongated and bipolar radial glia cell morphology as well as the round-shaped somata of neurons (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: Neurons in the CP and newborn neurons inside the VZ showed high intensity somatic signals.
source: Additionally, neurons in the CP and newborn neurons inside the VZ showed high intensity somatic signals (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: Strong THG signal is mostly detected in the CP (DCX-rich, low cell density) rather than the VZ (DCX-negative, high cell density).
source: Our results confirmed that strong THG signal is mostly detected in the CP (DCX-rich, low cell density), rather than the VZ (DCX-negative, high cell density) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: More than 90% of GFP-positive cells in electroporated organoids are neurons.
source: We previously demonstrated that >90% of the GFP-positive cells in electroporated organoids are neurons (Delepine et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors (Delepine et al., 2021).

claim: Both WT and MT organoids in fixed and live conditions had >85% overlap between GFP and THG signals.
source: Three-dimensional imaging of cells in organoids (~2 mm thickness) revealed that both WT and MT organoids in fixed and live conditions had >85% overlap between GFP and THG signals (Figure 2—figure supplements 2–5, see Methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 2–5.

claim: The maximum imaging depth was limited by the working distance of the objective, which was approximately 2 mm.
source: The maximum imaging depth was only limited by the working distance of the objective, which was approximately 2 mm in our experiments (Figure 3—video 3).
evidence: This is a technical limitation of the microscope system demonstrated experimentally.

claim: The extinction length of a fixed WT organoid is 162.5 µm at 1300 nm excitation wavelength.
source: Our label-free THG imaging characterization shows that the extinction lengths of a fixed WT and a MT organoid are 162.5 µm and 148.2 µm, respectively which are approximately half of the extinction length of a primary visual cortex of an awake mouse brain (Yildirim et al., 2019; Yildirim et al., 2020; Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: The extinction length of a fixed MT organoid is 148.2 µm at 1300 nm excitation wavelength.
source: Our label-free THG imaging characterization shows that the extinction lengths of a fixed WT and a MT organoid are 162.5 µm and 148.2 µm, respectively which are approximately half of the extinction length of a primary visual cortex of an awake mouse brain (Yildirim et al., 2019; Yildirim et al., 2020; Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Fixed WT and MT organoids are at least two times more scattering than the mouse visual cortex at 1300 nm excitation wavelength.
source: In other words, fixed WT and MT organoids are at least two times more scattering than the mouse visual cortex at 1300 nm excitation wavelength.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of extinction lengths measured experimentally.

claim: Average extinction length of WT organoids (152.1±3.5 µm) is significantly higher than that of MT organoids (125.9±4.9 µm).
source: Our results show that average extinction length of WT organoids (152.1±3.5 µm) is significantly higher than that of MT organoids (125.9±4.9 µm, p<0.005, n=6 organoids, t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis (p<0.005, n=6 organoids, t-test).

claim: RTT-MT organoids showed slightly (but not significantly) higher volumes than control organoids (1.13±0.18 × 10^7 µm³ for RTT-WT, and 1.39±0.15 × 10^7 µm³ for RTT-MT organoids, p=0.3013).
source: First, we quantified the total volume of each region of interest and found slightly (but not significantly) higher volumes in mutant organoids than in control ones (1.13±0.18 × 107 µm3 for RTT-WT, and 1.39±0.15 × 107 µm3 for RTT-MT organoids, p=0.3013; n=10 organoids, t-test; Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The surface area of the VZ region in RTT-MT organoids (11.0±0.71 × 10^5 µm²) was significantly higher than that in RTT-WT organoids (5.70±0.75 × 10^5 µm², p<0.0001).
source: However, the surface area of the VZ region in RTT-MT organoids was significantly higher than that in RTT-WT organoids (5.70±0.75 × 105 µm2 for RTT-WT, and 11.0±0.71 × 105 µm2 for RTT-MT organoids, p<0.0001; n=10 organoids, t-test; Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis (p<0.0001, n=10 organoids, t-test) shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The VZ thickness in RTT-MT organoids (9.99±0.27 µm) was significantly lower than that in RTT-WT organoids (23.11±4.12 µm, p<0.0001).
source: In addition, the ratio of volume to area was used as a relative measure of the VZ thickness. The progenitor-rich structures in the RTT-MT organoids had significantly lower unit thickness relative to RTT-WT organoids (23.11±4.12 µm for RTT-WT, and 9.99±0.27 µm for RTT-MT organoids, p<0.0001, n=10 organoids, t-test; Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis (p<0.0001, n=10 organoids, t-test) shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The number of ventricles was significantly higher in RTT-MT organoids (22.0±1.3) than in RTT-WT organoids (12.3±0.7, p<0.0001).
source: Finally, the number of ventricles was significantly higher in RTT-MT organoids (12.3±0.7 for RTT-WT, and 22.0±1.3 for RTT-MT organoids, p<0.0001, n=10 organoids, t-test; Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis (p<0.0001, n=10 organoids, t-test) shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The average migration speed in RTT-WT organoids was 23.4±0.2 µm/hr.
source: Specifically, we observed in RTT-WT organoids an average migration speed of 23.4±0.2 µm/hr (n=6 organoids, N=208 cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from live cell tracking (n=6 organoids, N=208 cells).

claim: The average migration speed in RTT-MT organoids was 13.3±0.1 µm/hour.
source: In contrast, RTT-MT cells had a reduced average speed of 13.3±0.1 µm/hour (n=6 organoids, N=217 cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from live cell tracking (n=6 organoids, N=217 cells).

claim: The average speed values in wild-type organoids are comparable to the speed recorded in neurons migrating off a human wild-type cerebral organoid onto a Matrigel-coated surface and in ferret cortical explants.
source: These average speed values are comparable to the speed recorded in neurons migrating off a human wild-type cerebral organoid onto a Matrigel-coated surface (Bershteyn et al., 2017) and in ferret cortical explants (Gertz and Kriegstein, 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison to prior work cited (Bershteyn et al., 2017; Gertz and Kriegstein, 2015).

claim: RTT-WT cells had significantly more straight trajectories (straightness value of 0.881±0.004) than RTT-MT cells (0.658±0.006).
source: With a straightness value close to 1, RTT-WT cells (straightness value of 0.881±0.004) had significantly more straight trajectories than RTT-MT cells (0.658±0.006) which showed much more nonlinear migrating patterns (Figure 5A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and C.

claim: Net displacement of MT cells (133.2±2.4 µm) was significantly lower than that of WT cells (244.4±3.6 µm).
source: Since the average speed of RTT-MT was lower and these cells had a less straight trajectory, net displacement of MT cells (133.2±2.4 µm) was significantly lower than that of WT cells (244.4±3.6 µm) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Imaging live organoids in the mini-incubator with three-photon microscopy did not induce any significant cell death compared to organoids that were not kept in the mini-incubator or imaged.
source: Our results show that imaging live organoids in the mini-incubator with three-photon microscopy did not induce any significant cell death compared to that in organoids that were not kept in the mini-incubator or imaged (Figure 5—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Caspase3 immunostaining shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 6.

claim: 23/25 GFP-positive cells in WT organoids emitted somatic THG signals.
source: Indeed, we found that 23/25 GFP-positive cells in the WT organoids and 27/30 cells in the MT organoids emitted somatic THG signals (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: 27/30 GFP-positive cells in MT organoids emitted somatic THG signals.
source: Indeed, we found that 23/25 GFP-positive cells in the WT organoids and 27/30 cells in the MT organoids emitted somatic THG signals (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Cells expressing both GFP and THG signal demonstrated similar migration deficits in their migration speeds as described with THG-only tracking.
source: Cells expressing both GFP and THG signal demonstrated similar migration deficits in their migration speeds (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C-D) as described above (Figures 5–6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4C-D and Figures 5-6.

claim: VZ expansion is uniquely different in human versus mouse neurogenesis.
source: As VZ expansion is uniquely different in human versus mouse neurogenesis (Florio and Huttner, 2014), it is likely that this phenotype would go unobserved in mouse (or other lissencephalic) models of RTT.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Florio and Huttner, 2014).

claim: The VZ expansion phenotype would likely go unobserved in mouse or other lissencephalic models of RTT.
source: As VZ expansion is uniquely different in human versus mouse neurogenesis (Florio and Huttner, 2014), it is likely that this phenotype would go unobserved in mouse (or other lissencephalic) models of RTT.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differences between human and mouse neurogenesis.

claim: Impaired proliferation of the progenitor pool and delayed maturation and presumed migration of neurons have been suggested in mice after in utero electroporation of Mecp2-sh RNA and in human RTT cerebral organoids.
source: Moreover, we and others previously suggested with endpoint experiments that the putative migration of young neurons through the VZ is impaired in mice after in utero electroporation of Mecp2-sh RNA as well as in human RTT cerebral organoids (Mellios et al., 2011; Bedogni et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Mellios et al., 2011; Bedogni et al., 2016).

claim: Lower migration speed and tortuous migration patterns were common in MT organoids regardless of the range of radial thickness.
source: Although there was a range of radial thickness in MT organoids, lower migration speed and tortuous migration patterns were common.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations across multiple organoids.

claim: Altered cytoskeleton dynamics have been previously suggested in rat, mouse and human models of Rett syndrome and could contribute to migration defects.
source: Altered cytoskeleton dynamics have been previously suggested in rat, mouse and human models of Rett syndrome and could contribute to migration defects (Kaufmann et al., 1995; Delépine et al., 2013; Delépine et al., 2016; Cortelazzo et al., 2014; Bhattacherjee et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and represents speculation about mechanisms.

claim: Non-cell autonomous effects such as impaired cell-to-cell communication, adhesion and radial glia dysfunction could contribute to the neuronal radial migration deficit.
source: Non-cell autonomous effects could also contribute to the neuronal radial migration deficit, such as impaired cell-to-cell communication, adhesion and radial glia dysfunction.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms underlying the observed migration deficits.

claim: Changes in ventricular wall thickness result not only from decreased neurogenesis and increased proliferation of the progenitor pool but also from abnormally slow displacement and tortuous trajectory of neurons.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that changes in ventricular wall thickness result not only from the decreased neurogenesis and increased proliferation of the progenitor pool but also from the abnormally slow displacement and tortuous trajectory of the neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The findings directly demonstrate dynamic deficits in migration at very early stages of prenatal development which provide insight into previously described deficits in human RTT brains.
source: Importantly, our findings directly demonstrate dynamic deficits in migration at very early stages of prenatal development which provide insight into previously described deficits in human RTT brains, including reduced cortical thickness, cell size and dendritic arborization, and reduced cerebral volume (Armstrong et al., 1995; Bauman et al., 1995; Carter et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current findings to prior observations in RTT patients.

claim: The optimized three-photon microscopy system can provide a new platform for monitoring structural and functional abnormalities in fixed and live organoids derived from patients with neurogenetic disorders.
source: We believe that our optimized three-photon microscopy system is straightforward to use, and can provide a new platform for monitoring structural and functional abnormalities in fixed and live organoids derived from patients with neurogenetic disorders as well as for therapeutic drug screening.
evidence: This is speculation about potential future applications of the technology.

claim: The system can be used for therapeutic drug screening.
source: We believe that our optimized three-photon microscopy system is straightforward to use, and can provide a new platform for monitoring structural and functional abnormalities in fixed and live organoids derived from patients with neurogenetic disorders as well as for therapeutic drug screening.
evidence: This is speculation about potential future applications of the technology.

claim: The system can study phenotypes in calcium activity in neurons, especially VZ calcium dynamics such as waves.
source: In addition, we can study phenotypes in calcium activity in neurons especially VZ calcium dynamics such as waves (Weissman et al., 2004) as well as their migration deficits in cerebral organoids.
evidence: This is speculation about potential future applications with citation to prior work on calcium waves (Weissman et al., 2004).

claim: The system can capture structural phenotypes in myelinated axons and endothelial cells (microvasculature).
source: In addition, we can capture structural phenotypes in myelinated axons and endothelial cells (microvasculature; Yildirim et al., 2020).
evidence: This is speculation about potential future applications with citation to prior work (Yildirim et al., 2020).

claim: Imaging myelinated axons and endothelial cells can be used for studying brain disorders such as Multiple Sclerosis and Alzheimer's disease with cerebral organoids.
source: We believe that imaging myelinated axons as well as endothelial cells can be used for studying brain disorders such as Multiple Sclerosis and Alzheimer's disease with cerebral organoids since there is a significant loss of myelin as well as reduction of blood flow in these diseases, respectively.
evidence: This is speculation about potential future applications based on known disease pathology.

claim: It should be possible to perform structural and functional three-photon and THG imaging for revealing structural and functional phenotypes for cancer applications such as glioblastoma.
source: Finally, it should be possible to perform structural and functional three-photon and THG imaging for revealing structural and functional phenotypes for cancer applications such as glioblastoma (Bakker et al., 2022).
evidence: This is speculation about potential future applications with citation to prior work (Bakker et al., 2022).

claim: The pulse width on the sample was approximately 250 fs due to dispersion in the microscope before optimization.
source: The internal compressor in NOPA could compress the Gaussian pulse width to 22 fs (which was the transform limited pulse width for 110 nm spectral full width half maximum bandwidth). Due to the dispersion in the microscope, the Gaussian pulse width on the sample was ~250 fs.
evidence: This is a description of the technical characteristics of the system before optimization.

claim: After dispersing the pulse with a 65 cm long prism-pair and silicon broadband window, the pulse width on the sample was reduced to 27 fs in the deepest part of the organoids.
source: After dispersing the pulse with 65 cm long prism-pair, and silicon broadband window (Thorlabs, WG81050) the pulse width on the sample was reduced to 27 fs in the deepest part of the organoids (pulse widths <30 fs obtained, to our knowledge, for the first time).
evidence: This is a description of the technical optimization achieved in the system.

claim: Pulse widths less than 30 fs were obtained for the first time in this type of imaging.
source: After dispersing the pulse with 65 cm long prism-pair, and silicon broadband window (Thorlabs, WG81050) the pulse width on the sample was reduced to 27 fs in the deepest part of the organoids (pulse widths <30 fs obtained, to our knowledge, for the first time).
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the technical achievement.

claim: The frame rate at 512 × 512 pixel resolution was increased up to 2 Hz by building a delay line to double the repetition rate.
source: In addition, we built a delay line to double the repetition rate thereby increasing the frame rate of THG imaging. Subsequently, the frame rate at 512 × 512 pixel resolution was increased up to 2 Hz.
evidence: This is a description of a technical improvement to the system.

claim: Laser power ranged from 0.5 to 5 mW at the sample depending on depth and fluorescence expression levels.
source: Laser power ranged from 0.5 to 5 mW at the sample depending on depth and fluorescence expression levels.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental parameters used.

claim: One pair of isogenic iPSC clonal lines (Line 1) was produced from an individual with RTT harboring a heterozygous single nucleotide deletion (frameshift 705delG) in the transcriptional repression domain of MeCP2.
source: One pair (Line 1) was produced as previously described (Mellios et al., 2011) from one individual with RTT harboring a heterozygous single nucleotide deletion (frameshift 705delG) in the transcriptional repression domain of MeCP2.
evidence: This is a description of the cell lines used in the study with citation to prior work (Mellios et al., 2011).

claim: The RTT-WT line expressed exclusively the wild-type allele of MECP2 while the RTT-MT line expressed exclusively the mutated allele due to monoallelic expression of X-chromosome genes and clonal selection of iPSCs.
source: Because of the monoallelic expression of X-chromosome genes and clonal selection of iPSCs, the 'RTT-WT' line expressed exclusively the wild-type allele of MECP2, while the "RTT-MT" line expressed exclusively the mutated allele.
evidence: This is a description of the characteristics of the cell lines based on X-inactivation.

claim: The second pair of isogenic iPSC clonal lines (Line 2) was from an individual with RTT harboring a heterozygous single nucleotide mutation MECP2R306C located in the transcriptional repression domain of MeCP2.
source: The second pair of isogenic iPSC clonal lines (Line 2), produced as previously described (Nott et al., 2016), was from another individual with RTT harboring a heterozygous single nucleotide mutation MECP2R306C located in the transcriptional repression domain (TRD) or more specifically NCoR/SMRT interaction domain (NID) of MeCP2, which selectively blocks its interaction with the NCoR/SMRT complex (Lyst and Bird, 2015; Lyst et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a description of the cell lines used in the study with citations to prior work (Nott et al., 2016; Lyst and Bird, 2015; Lyst et al., 2013).

claim: The MECP2R306C mutation selectively blocks MeCP2's interaction with the NCoR/SMRT complex.
source: The second pair of isogenic iPSC clonal lines (Line 2), produced as previously described (Nott et al., 2016), was from another individual with RTT harboring a heterozygous single nucleotide mutation MECP2R306C located in the transcriptional repression domain (TRD) or more specifically NCoR/SMRT interaction domain (NID) of MeCP2, which selectively blocks its interaction with the NCoR/SMRT complex (Lyst and Bird, 2015; Lyst et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Lyst and Bird, 2015; Lyst et al., 2013).

claim: The MECP2R306C RTT-WT line was generated from the MECP2R306C iPSCs using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing to correct the R306C mutation.
source: Because the MECP2R306C-derived iPSCs had skewed X-inactivation, and expressed only the MECP2R306C allele, the MECP2R306C RTT-WT line was generated from the MECP2R306C iPSCs using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing to correct the R306C mutation (Nott et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of how the control line was generated with citation to prior work (Nott et al., 2016).

claim: Incubation of fixed organoids in H-protos index-matching solution for 3 hours resulted in improvement in maximum imaging depth up to 50% compared to the condition without incubation.
source: For imaging some of the fixed organoids, we incubated organoids in the H-protos index- matching solution for 3 hr. With this incubation, we observed improvement in maximum imaging depth up to 50% compared to the condition without the incubation (Figure 5—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 7.
